name: Diego Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing history and politics, and my flat is ten minutes from the lecture halls on Kestrel Street. Most weeks I have three lectures, two seminars and a lot of reading in the library with a paper notebook, because I still write everything by hand. On Thursdays I help at a student group that lobbies the university about rent. My dad's pharmacy pays for everything, so I don't have to work, and I feel a bit guilty about that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what do you want out of the degree, so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly I don't know yet. My results were average, so I wasn't sure I'd get in, and now I want it to lead to something like policy research or journalism. But I keep hearing those are the jobs AI goes after first, which makes me angry more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the hype was always oversold by the same companies that want our data. I'd tell my friends I told them so, and I'd post that the money should have gone to hospitals. At seminars I'd keep saying we should be learning to think, not typing prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my plan stays boring and fine. I'd finish the degree, apply for research assistant posts, and compete with everyone else who also got average marks. I'm not scared of AI in this one, I'm scared of the ordinary job market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to lectures and keep my handwritten notes. I'd join the student union committee next term, because I want a CV line that isn't just my grades. And I'd ask my tutor, Dr Haddad, about a summer placement at a think tank, probably this June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but a bit flat. Nothing is on fire, yet nothing looks easy either. I still have to prove myself with average results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad's money covers you. Does that change how worried you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, and I know it. If my dad stopped paying, I'd be in the cafe on Kestrel Street at six in the morning. Because of him I can afford to be worried about ideas rather than rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the boring version still leaves graduates without jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms that cut entry-level hiring to save money, and the government that lets them. I'd put it on the people who hold the budget, not on AI itself. A tool doesn't decide to skip hiring a graduate.

say: I'd tell friends the **hype** was oversold by companies who wanted our data.
I'd say at seminars that we should learn to **think**, not type prompts.
I'd post that the money should have gone to **hospitals**.
think: I'm not scared of AI here, I'm scared of an **ordinary** tight job market.
With average results I'll compete with plenty of people for **research** posts.
do: Keep going to lectures and keep **handwritten** notes.
Join the student union **committee** next term for a CV line.
Ask my tutor about a summer **placement** at a think tank in June.
feel: Relieved but a bit **flat**, since nothing is on fire and nothing is easy.
S0.quote: I'd put it on the people who hold the budget, not on AI itself. A tool doesn't decide to skip hiring a graduate.
fieldNote: **Resistant** and idealistic: refuses AI tools yet frames problems as politics and budgets.
Aware that his **father's** money lets him worry about ideas, not rent.
Main fear in this world is the **normal** graduate job market, not AI.

steps.text: Keep writing notes by hand and attending every seminar
Join the student union committee and push on rent
Ask Dr Haddad for a summer think tank placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need unions and rules, now, before the cuts. Writing, checking and planning are exactly what my degree trains. I'd go on the student radio and say universities should demand a say in how these tools are used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of the junior research and journalism jobs vanish before I graduate. Three years is not long. I'd be competing for fewer posts with an average degree, and I refuse to use the tools, which might look stubborn to employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep refusing for now, but I'd learn what the tools do so I can argue about them. I'd double my union and student politics work, and ask Dr Haddad how to get into policy through a public body, where hiring is slower to change. I'd also look at a master's, even though I don't love the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, with some worry underneath. I feel like I picked the one degree that the news says is first on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you refuse the tools. What happens if an employer asks for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn them at the last minute, like someone learning to drive for a new job. I just don't want to be the person who learned it first and made the cuts easier. Maybe that's pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about the master's idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say yes immediately. My dad would ask if it was a real plan or a way to hide from the job market. He'd be right to ask, and I'd probably say a bit of both.

say: I'd say we need **unions** and rules now, before the cuts come.
I'd argue on student radio that universities should have a say in these **tools**.
think: Many junior research and journalism jobs could **vanish** before I graduate.
My refusal to use AI might look **stubborn** to an employer.
do: Learn what the tools do so I can **argue** about them, not use them.
Double my union and student politics **work**.
Ask Dr Haddad about a public body route and a **master's**.
feel: Angry, with **worry** underneath, as if I picked the first degree on the list.
S1.quote: I just don't want to be the person who learned it first and made the cuts easier. Maybe that's pride.
fieldNote: His principles are real but he admits **pride** is part of the refusal.
Plans a **master's** and public body job as slower, safer ground.
Anger at firms covers a real **fear** about the next three years.

steps.text: Learn what AI writing tools do without relying on them
Double the hours spent on the student union campaign
Research master's degrees in public policy for next autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest political failure of my lifetime, because nobody voted for this speed. Two years means governments won't have a plan. I'd be at every protest and every meeting I could get to, and I'd tell friends to demand public ownership of the big systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my whole degree could be worth very little by the time I finish. By 2028 I'd be in my second year, and thinking jobs are gone first. My family's money helps, but my dad's pharmacy would change too, since checking prescriptions is thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop planning for graduation and start organising. I'd put my time into the student union and the party youth branch, and I'd ask my dad to hold his savings safe rather than expand the shop. I might drop out of the library routine and work for a campaign, because arguing for rules would matter more than a seminar mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry that it feels out of my hands. I'd have trouble sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay enrolled, because a degree still looks like a plan, but I'd stop caring about marks. Part of me wants to say I'd quit, and part of me knows I'm scared of telling my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about the pharmacy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't borrow to buy new equipment, and keep six months of costs in cash. He'd laugh at me for giving a pharmacist advice, then he'd probably do it.

say: I'd say nobody **voted** for this speed and governments have no plan.
I'd tell friends to demand **public** ownership of the biggest systems.
think: My whole degree could be worth **little** by the time I finish.
Even my dad's pharmacy changes, because checking prescriptions is **thinking** work.
do: Stop planning for graduation and start **organising** through the union.
Ask my dad to hold his savings in **cash** instead of expanding the shop.
Stay enrolled but stop caring about **marks**.
feel: Frightened, angry, and **powerless**, with trouble sleeping.
S2.quote: Part of me wants to say I'd quit, and part of me knows I'm scared of telling my mum.
fieldNote: Moves from principle to **activism** fast; family money gives him room to act.
Tells his father to keep **cash**, showing care for the family business.
Admits he would **stay** enrolled because a degree still looks like a plan.

steps.text: Spend most evenings organising with the student union
Join the party youth branch and attend weekly meetings
Ask Dad to keep six months of shop costs in cash
Stay enrolled but stop chasing marks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to fight for rules, but only if we start now. I'd write to my representative about retraining funds and a shorter working week. At seminars I'd say the degree is still worth having, because you need people who can question the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have a small window. By 2031 I'd have just graduated, straight into the worst year to look for a thinking job. I'd also feel my progressive side isn't just talk, because policy is the one thing that might change the outcome.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and use the next three years to build real contacts in unions and policy groups. I'd take a part-time paid role at the union research office when one opens, and I'd learn basic data skills in my second year. I'd keep my notes by hand but I'd take one data course this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strangely focused. It's frightening, but five years gives me something to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the data course a change from how you've been?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one, yes. I used to say I'd never touch anything near AI, but a spreadsheet course isn't the same as a chatbot. It's a way to say I changed my mind a little without saying it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your government to do in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay people to retrain, and tax the companies that gain. Also make sure new graduates get guaranteed places in public service training, so we aren't left to compete on a blank CV.

I'd tell seminars the degree still matters because we need people who **question** machines.
think: By 2031 I'd have just graduated, into the **worst** year to find thinking work.
Policy is the one thing that might change the **outcome**.
do: Build contacts in unions and policy groups over **three** years.
Take a part-time job at the union **research** office when it opens.
feel: Strangely **focused**, because five years gives me something to aim at.
S3.quote: A spreadsheet course isn't the same as a chatbot. It's a way to say I changed my mind a little without saying it out loud.
fieldNote: Softens his stance slightly; the **data** course is a face-saving compromise.
Uses the **five-year** window to build a union and policy network.
Wants **public** retraining and graduate guarantees rather than individual fixes.

steps.text: Write to my representative about funded retraining places
Take a paid part-time job at the union research office
Enrol in a spreadsheet and data course this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the version where we can still get it right. Plenty of time to vote, organise and pass laws. I'd tell my friends this is when we should be building the public systems that share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me less scared for myself. I'd graduate, work for a few years, and by 2036 I'd be about 28 and probably settled somewhere. But I'd worry for people who aren't in a family like mine, who won't have a cushion while everything shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take the policy research route, and maybe do a master's in my third year. I'd stay active in the union, and when I'm working I'd join a staff union straight away. I'd also learn to use AI tools at work, because by then refusing would be a luxury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. A decade makes it feel like something I can help shape rather than just survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you less angry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly. The anger just changes from panic to impatience, because I want the government to start acting today and not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you would change in your own life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating my refusal to use AI as a badge. In ten years it'll be as normal as email, and I'd rather understand it well enough to criticise it properly.

say: I'd say ten years is the version where we can still get it **right**.
I'd tell friends to build public **systems** that share the gains.
think: A decade makes me less **scared** for myself but I worry about people without a cushion.
By 2036 I'd be about 28 and probably **settled** somewhere.
do: Finish the degree and aim for **policy** research work.
Join a staff **union** the day I start a job.
Start using AI tools at **work**, since refusing would be a luxury.
feel: Calmer than in the others, as if I could help **shape** it.
S4.quote: I'd stop treating my refusal to use AI as a badge. In ten years it'll be as normal as email
fieldNote: A decade turns panic into **impatience** and lets him drop the refusal as a badge.
His concern shifts to **people** without a family cushion.
Still **uneasy** about a long-term job market, even with time.

steps.text: Finish the history and politics degree and apply for research posts
Join a staff union in the first week of any job
Learn AI tools well enough to criticise them at work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, by far. Two years doesn't give anybody time to build rules or retrain, and I'd be stuck in the middle of my degree. What would help is a government plan that is real and public, with guaranteed training and a support payment, so nobody has to rely on a family like mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know my views are easy to hold when my dad pays the bills. I'd like the next person you talk to to not take that for granted.

headlineQuote: If my dad stopped paying, I'd be in the cafe on Kestrel Street at six in the morning.
portrait: Diego is an 18-year-old **history** and politics student whose father's pharmacy pays for his flat and fees.
He refuses AI tools out of principle, writes notes by hand, and blames **firms** and governments rather than the technology.
He turns worry into **organising**: student union, a party youth branch and letters to his representative.
His mood climbs to **alarmed** in the 2-year world and softens as the warning time grows.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries him most, because two years leaves no time to build rules or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A real, public **plan** with guaranteed training and a support payment, so nobody depends on family money.
